description: The objective of Reading Comprehension is to test the ability to read, understand, and logically analyze a given passage. For accuracy in competitive exams, understanding the main idea and the author's tone is highly essential.

sections.title: Core Concepts and Passage Structure
sections.description: Before solving questions from any passage, it is important to understand its basic structure, subject matter, and the author's purpose.

key_concepts.explanation: This is the central theme or main point of the passage. The entire passage is written to explain, argue, or support this specific idea.
This reflects the author's feelings toward the subject. The tone can be positive, negative, critical, sarcastic, or informative/neutral.
Information that is not directly stated in the passage but can be logically deduced based on the provided facts and clues.

strategies.title: Importance of First and Last Paragraphs
strategies.detail: The main idea of the passage is usually clearly stated in the first paragraph (the introduction) or the last paragraph (the conclusion). Focus heavily on these areas.

sections.title: Main Types of Questions
sections.description: Various types of questions are asked in reading comprehension, and the approach to solving each type requires a different strategy.

question_types.explanation: These questions are based on specific information, dates, names, or figures explicitly given in the passage.
question_types.approach: Identify the primary keywords in the question and scan the passage for them to locate the direct answer.

question_types.explanation: The answer to these questions is not directly found in the text. You must draw a logical deduction based on the provided information.
question_types.approach: Eliminate options that go beyond the scope of the passage or use extreme wording. Choose only the option that is strictly and logically supported by the text.

question_types.explanation: These questions relate to the meaning or opposite of a specific word as it is used in the passage.
question_types.approach: Instead of relying purely on the literal meaning of the word, read the sentence where it appears to understand its contextual meaning.

sections.title: Transition Words and Logical Clues
sections.description: Transition words show the relationship between sentences and help the reader track the direction of the author's thoughts.

key_indicators.usage_hint: These words indicate that the author is shifting away from their previous thought. The tone or direction of the passage changes immediately after these words.
These words state the reason behind an event or its final result. They are crucial clues for inference and conclusion-based questions.
These words indicate that the author is reinforcing the same point or idea with additional examples. There is no change in narrative direction.

examples.incorrect_or_context: The government launched a massive employment scheme. However, the unemployment rate continued to rise.
examples.correct_or_usage: The use of 'However' clearly establishes a contrast between effort and outcome.
examples.explanation: In this context, 'However' signals that despite a positive initial effort (employment scheme), the resulting outcome was negative (rising unemployment). Catching these shifts is essential for accurate comprehension.

sections.title: Reading Strategies and Time Management
sections.description: Using effective reading strategies is absolutely necessary to solve passages quickly and with high accuracy.

strategies.title: Skimming for the Gist
strategies.detail: Instead of reading the entire passage word-for-word initially, quickly read the main ideas, topic sentences, and the beginnings and ends of paragraphs to grasp the core theme.

strategies.title: Previewing the Questions
strategies.detail: Take a quick glance at the questions (without reading the options) before you start the passage. This primes your brain to look for specific details while reading.

strategies.title: Elimination Method
strategies.detail: For multiple-choice questions (MCQs), proactively eliminate options that are out of scope, contradict the passage, or contain extreme modifier words like 'Always', 'Never', or 'Only'.

exceptions.condition: Highly Philosophical, Abstract, or Dense Passages
exceptions.explanation: If the language of the passage is exceptionally difficult and skimming does not clarify the overall meaning, do not waste excessive time trying to decode the entire text.
exceptions.example: In such extreme cases, attempt only the specific fact-based and vocabulary questions, and skip the complex inference-based questions to maximize your time management elsewhere.
